title: Elements and Compounds
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 8 Integrated Science; not yet checked by a CBC Integrated Science teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Use bottle-top or plasticine models: one colour for one kind of atom. Iron filings and sulphur mixed (separable with a magnet) next to a picture of iron sulphide (not separable) show mixture against compound. Real packets (salt, toothpaste, a soda can) give elements on labels.

skills.key_step: The child tells the four apart with a model: an atom (one particle), an element (one kind of atom), a molecule (atoms joined) and a compound (different elements joined chemically), and keeps a compound apart from a mixture.

floor.prerequisite: Knows air is a mixture of gases.
floor.question: Name one gas in air.

representations: iron filings with sulphur and a magnet
a four-box chart: atom, element, molecule, compound
steps: An element: many balls, all one colour.
A molecule: balls joined (two of a colour for oxygen gas, mixed colours for water).
A compound: different elements joined; not separable like a mixture.

board.do: Draw two red balls joined and one red with two white joined.

misconceptions.ask: Is one ball the same as two joined?
misconceptions.repair: An atom is one particle; a molecule is atoms joined.

listen_for: a compound is one kind of atom
misconceptions.ask: What colours are the balls in water?
misconceptions.repair: A compound has different elements joined.

misconceptions.ask: Can a magnet pull iron out of iron sulphide?
misconceptions.repair: In a compound the elements are joined chemically.

misconceptions.ask: How many kinds of atom are in oxygen gas?

checks.question: Is water an element or a compound?
What is a molecule?
checks.answer: two or more atoms joined together

skills.key_step: The child gives the symbols of common elements with a capital first letter and a small second letter, including the Latin ones (Fe, Na, K, Cu, Ag, Au).
representations: symbol cards with names on the back
CO and Co written side by side
steps: Most: the first letter (H, O, C, N).
Some: first two letters (Ca, Mg, Al, Cl).
Latin ones: Fe (ferrum), Na (natrium), K (kalium), Cu, Ag, Au.
contexts: Fe on a cereal box (iron added)
Au on a gold price board

board.do: Wait for "no, the small letter matters".
Ask the child to write the symbols for iron and sodium.

misconceptions.ask: What is the Latin name for iron?
What is the symbol for calcium?
misconceptions.repair: K is potassium; calcium is Ca.

misconceptions.ask: What is the Latin word for gold?
misconceptions.repair: Gold is Au (aurum); silver is Ag.

checks.question: What is the symbol for sodium?
Which element has the symbol Cu?

skills.key_step: The child writes a word equation with the reactants on the left, an arrow, and the product named from its elements with the -ide ending (magnesium + oxygen gives magnesium oxide).

floor.prerequisite: Can tell an element from a compound.
floor.question: Is magnesium oxide an element or a compound?

representations: burning magnesium (teacher) and the white powder
steps: Write what we start with (reactants), joined by +.
Name the product: metal name first, then -ide.
contexts: rust forming on a mabati roof

board.do: Ask what the product is called.

misconceptions.repair: Reactants on the left, product on the right.

misconceptions.ask: How many elements are in the product?
What did the scale show after rusting?
Is the white powder still shiny metal?
misconceptions.repair: The product is a new compound with a new name.

checks.question: Write the word equation for carbon burning in oxygen.
What is made when sodium reacts with chlorine?

skills.key_step: The child says what common elements are used for and why (copper for wires: conducts; aluminium for pans and foil: light; iron for building: strong; chlorine for treating water; carbon as charcoal; oxygen in hospitals) and reads elements on packaging labels.

floor.prerequisite: Can give the symbols of common elements.
floor.question: What is the symbol for copper?

representations: objects: a copper wire, foil, a nail, charcoal
steps: Name the element in the object.
Say the property that makes it fit.
Read labels for elements and safety notes.

board.do: Draw a wire, a sufuria and a nail.

board.say: Which element, and why that one?

board.do: Wait for "copper, it carries electricity well".
Ask the child to add the element and property for the other two.

misconceptions.ask: Which metal is inside electric cables?
What does this label say about the contents and date?
misconceptions.repair: Labels give contents, amounts, dates and safety.

listen_for: chlorine is safe, it is in salt
misconceptions.ask: What does the chlorine label warn?
misconceptions.repair: Chlorine gas is toxic; salt is a safe compound.

checks.question: Why is copper used for electric wires?
Name one element used to treat drinking water.
